text.p: The following are some of the leading stories in Finnish papers this morning.
HELSINGIN SANOMAT
- Investors have not sought new forms of investments despite the abolition of tax-free high-interest deposits.

- Former governor of the Bank of Finland Rolf Kullberg, reacting to criticism from former president Mauno Koivisto, says it was wise to link the markka to the European currency unit in 1991 with no change in the exchange rate.
- Mother's milk contaminated with environmental pollutant dioxin can permanently damage childrens' teeth, study shows. @
- Police and customs say volume of illicit drugs confiscated is less than reported crime rates.
DEMARI
- Social policy issues have been ignored in EMU discussions, says Turku university professor Kari Salavuo.
- City of Helsinki is seeing rapid growth in poverty. Twenty percent of the inhabitants receive minimum unemployment benefit as only form of support.
KAUPPALEHTI
- State will not easily give up the 1.5 percent stamp-tax on bank credits, finance ministry says. Tax, which banks say is unfair, brings revenues of 700 million markka. @
- American Global Finance magazine gave Bank of Finland governor Sirkka Hamalainen a "very good" rating for her performance, ranking her 19th out of 34 central bank leaders.
- Finnish sawmills have put the worst behind them, but markets recovering slowly, says one forest industry official.
- Shoe manufacturer Pertti Palmroth wants to keep production in Finland, but says skilled workers hard to find.
AAMULEHTI
- Defence Minister Anneli Taina says does not fear that door to NATO will be shut after just one round of enlargement.
- Tyre recycling off to good start at six regional centres. @
- Surveillance cameras at intersections have curbed drivers' running through red lights.
- Board recyclers have settled price dispute with industry, which has insisted on lower prices.
- Artist Katarina Reuter wins 150,000 markka art award.
TURUN SANOMAT
- Wihuri-yhtyma may be interested in buying Kesko's TukoSpar unit, chairman Antti Aarnio-Wihuri says. Swedish ICA says it is not interested.
- Finnish post office plans to make Santa Claus letter service a profitable business in next few years.
